Question 4 — the mechanics

  • The 2×2 estimate is the interaction coefficient in reg y i.treated##i.post — four means with a standard error.
  • Cluster at the level at which treatment was assigned: the district.

Today’s question: on Day 1 the map had a single red “program starts” line. Today every cohort has its own.

What happens to the map — and who, exactly, is the control group?

Part 1 — The obvious thing, and what it returns

Load Day 1’s panel

use "${der}/day1_panel.dta", clear
xtset district_id year
gen byte treat = (year >= adopt_year) & !missing(adopt_year)
  • Same panel as Day 1 — nothing to rebuild.
  • One new variable: treat switches on at each district’s own adoption year. That one line is the whole generalization.

Where we left off

Day 1: 2007 cohort vs never-treated — clean event study, flat pre-trends, effect growing to ~9.5 points.

But we threw away three quarters of the data.

table (adopt_year) if year == 2019, stat(freq)
adopt_year |
  2007     |     45
  2010     |     45
  2013     |     45
  2016     |     30
      .    |     15

Staggered adoption — the most common setting in real policy work.

All five groups

The obvious generalization

Day 1’s regression never mentioned a start date:

\[ y_{it} = \alpha_i + \lambda_t + \beta D_{it} + \varepsilon_{it} \]

\(D_{it}\) just switches on when district \(i\) adopts.

So do what almost every paper did from 1994 to ~2018 — run it on the full panel:

areg emp_rate treat i.year, absorb(district_id) cluster(district_id)

The result

       treat |   .1024949   .1858339     0.55   0.582

0.10 points. p = 0.58.

On Day 1, a quarter of this data gave 5.59, highly significant.

With four times the data, the effect has vanished.

Something is wrong. The question is what.

Build the event-study dummies

Same trick as Day 1 — two changes: rel now exists for every adopting district, and the leads run the full −12 … −2.

gen rel = year - adopt_year

forvalues k = 12(-1)2 {
    qui gen byte lead_`k' = (rel == -`k') & !missing(rel)
}
forvalues k = 0/12 {
    qui gen byte lag_`k'  = (rel ==  `k') & !missing(rel)
}

(Leave leads out and they quietly join the comparison group — biasing everything.)

Check the assumption — the way we learned on Day 1

areg emp_rate lead_* lag_* i.year, ///
    absorb(district_id) cluster(district_id)
   k = -12   coef =   1.565   se = 0.326   p = 0.000   <-- significant
   k = - 9   coef =   1.177   se = 0.258   p = 0.000   <-- significant
   k = - 5   coef =   1.032   se = 0.205   p = 0.000   <-- significant
   k = - 2   coef =   0.763   se = 0.195   p = 0.000   <-- significant

Every one of the eleven pre-period coefficients is significant.

The picture

Treated districts appear to have been on a higher path for a decade before adopting anything.

Before you see the next slide

Write down your answer.

You have: an estimate near zero, and an event study that fails the pre-trend check everywhere.

What do you conclude, and what do you do next?

We move on when everyone has something on paper.

Part 2 — The reveal

This data is simulated

We know the true effect for every district in every year — it was written into the data before anything was estimated.

  TRUE average treatment effect on the treated :  3.946
  Pre-period observations with a non-zero effect:    0
  • The program worked: 3.95 points. The static regression said 0.10 — about 2.6% of the truth.
  • Parallel trends holds exactly — zero pre-period effects anywhere. The pre-trend you found does not exist.

What is actually in the data

 adopt_year |   Mean tau
  2007      |    5.885
  2010      |    3.575
  2013      |    2.000
  2016      |    1.000

Two things, both true of most real rollouts:

  1. Effects grow over time — capacity takes years to build.
  2. Cohorts differ — early adopters gain more.

Both are normal. Neither breaks parallel trends.

The lesson: the estimator was broken — and so was the test you used to check it. Both pointed at the same wrong conclusion.

Why it breaks: Goodman-Bacon (2021)

The static TWFE estimate is a weighted average of every possible 2×2 in the data.

It needs a balanced panel — drop districts with gaps, and say so:

bysort district_id: egen byte anymiss = max(missing(emp_rate))
keep if anymiss == 0
bacondecomp emp_rate treat, ddetail
  Districts dropped to balance the panel: 46 of 180

The estimate being decomposed is therefore 0.190, not 0.102.

The decomposition

Comparison type Sign of every term Weight Legitimate?
Never_v_timing positive (+2.77) 22% yes
Early_v_Late positive (+0.88 to +4.19) ~33% yes
Late_v_Early negative (−0.94 to −4.54) ~45% no

Nearly half the estimate comes from comparisons that should never happen — and they push the estimate down, nearly wiping out the real effect.

Every 2×2, plotted

Above the dashed line: the legitimate comparisons. Below: already-treated districts used as controls — wrong sign, heavy weights.

The dashed line is their weighted average: 0.19 — next to nothing.

Why “already treated” controls are poison

Compare a 2013 adopter against a 2007 adopter: the 2007 district plays control — but its outcome is still rising from its own treatment.

Subtract one treated group’s rise from another’s, and you remove the very thing you are measuring.

Because effects grow, the “control” rises faster than the “treated” — and the comparison turns negative.

The same contamination created the fake pre-trend.

Part 3 — Rebuilding the estimator

By hand: Day 1’s 2×2, one cohort at a time

Rule: never use an already-treated district as a control.

\[ \widehat{ATT}(g,t) = \big(\bar y_{g,t} - \bar y_{g,g-1}\big) - \big(\bar y_{\text{never},t} - \bar y_{\text{never},g-1}\big) \]

A loop over cohorts and years; four sample means per cell; post the result.

The loop

foreach g of local cohorts {
    forvalues t = `g'/`tmax' {
        local base = `g' - 1
        qui sum emp_rate if adopt_year == `g' & year == `t'
        local a1 = r(mean)                        // treated, after
        qui sum emp_rate if adopt_year == `g' & year == `base'
        local a0 = r(mean)                        // treated, before
        qui sum emp_rate if missing(adopt_year) & year == `t'
        local c1 = r(mean)                        // never-treated, after
        qui sum emp_rate if missing(adopt_year) & year == `base'
        local c0 = r(mean)                        // never-treated, before
        post `M' (`g') (`t') ((`a1'-`a0')-(`c1'-`c0'))
    }
}

Four sums per cell — the four means of a 2×2. Base year g − 1; controls never-treated only. (Abridged; full version in day2.do.)

What the loop returns

  Hand-built overall ATT =  3.864   (truth:  3.946)

  | 2007     5.370      5.904 |
  | 2010     4.283      3.563 |
  | 2013     1.783      2.006 |
  | 2016     0.506      0.998 |

No package. Just sample means.

TWFE was off by a factor of forty; this simple loop lands within 0.1 of the truth — and ranks the cohorts correctly.

Doing it properly: csdid (Callaway & Sant’Anna 2021)

gen gvar = cond(missing(adopt_year), 0, adopt_year)
csdid emp_rate, ivar(district_id) time(year) gvar(gvar) notyet
estat simple
         ATT |   3.951182   .2079284    19.00   0.000

  >>> TRUE ATT =  3.946
  • gvar(): adoption cohort, 0 = never treated.
  • notyet: not-yet-treated units may serve as controls — buys precision.
  • What it will never do: use an already-treated unit as a control.

The event study, done right

estat event, window(-8 12)
     Pre_avg |  -.0032269   .0321131    -0.10   0.920
    Post_avg |   5.203305   .1778835    29.25   0.000

Same data — and the pre-trend that was significant at every lead has disappeared.

Nothing about the districts changed. Only which comparisons the estimator was allowed to make.

The picture

Honest caveat: Tm8, Tm7, Tm1 are individually significant — eight tests, 15 never-treated districts, some come up by chance.

Roth (2022): don’t judge a design by individual leads — they are noisy, in both directions.

Pre_avg = −0.003 (p = 0.92) is the informative summary.

Three estimators, one dataset

  |         Static TWFE   0.102   0.186 |
  | Hand-built ATT(g,t)   3.864       . |
  |               csdid   3.951   0.208 |

One question. Three answers. Two of them right.

Part 4 — The table, regenerated

Every number in Day 1’s table is now wrong

Headline 0.10 → 3.95; new estimator; new sample; new standard errors.

If Table 1 lived in Word, you would be retyping all of it tonight.

eststo d1: qui areg emp_rate treat i.year, ///
    absorb(district_id) cluster(district_id)
qui csdid emp_rate, ivar(district_id) time(year) ///
    gvar(gvar) notyet agg(simple)
eststo d2
qui csdid emp_rate, ivar(district_id) time(year) ///
    gvar(gvar) agg(simple)
eststo d3

Then Day 1’s pattern — one options macro, three outputs:

esttab d1 d2 d3, `topts'
esttab d1 d2 d3 using "${res}/table2_staggered.rtf", replace `topts' ///
    title("The childcare program under three estimators")

The one thing that will trip you up

csdid + estat simple does not post estimates for esttab:

. esttab .
estimates __000002 not found
r(111);

This error is what pushes people into clumsy workarounds (parmest, matrices).

You don’t need them. The fix is the agg(simple) option — it stores the overall ATT like a normal regression result, so eststo/esttab just work.

The coefficient is named ATT, so rename(treat DiD ATT DiD) puts everything on one row — exactly Day 1’s trick.

Table 2

                                (1)             (2)             (3)
----------------------------------------------------------------------
Childcare program             0.102           3.951***        4.010***
                            (0.186)         (0.208)         (0.241)
----------------------------------------------------------------------
Estimator               Static TWFE    Callaway-Sant'Anna  Callaway-Sant'Anna
Comparison group    All other districts   Not-yet-treated  Never-treated only
Observations                   2827            2782            2782

Columns 2 vs 3: notyet bought precision (0.208 vs 0.241) without costing accuracy — both bracket the truth.

Showing both is how you demonstrate the result does not depend on the choice.

One command rebuilds everything

do master.do
  • checks packages first (csdid drdid bacondecomp estout), fails loudly
  • one global root — the only absolute path in the project
  • rebuilds both days: data, seven figures, two tables, Word + LaTeX

If reproducing your project means remembering which files to run in which order, you will eventually break it — usually when a referee asks for one more column.

What changed, and when

The history in one slide

  • Card & Krueger (1994): one treated state, one control, one date. Day 1’s 2×2 was the complete, correct tool.
  • 1994–2018: the profession ran areg y treat i.year, absorb(id) on staggered rollouts and read \(\beta\) as an average effect.
  • Goodman-Bacon (2021): it usually isn’t one.

The modern literature is not a replacement for DiD.

It is the same idea, protected from the ways the simple version fails.

The rule to leave with

Units adopt at different times → do not report static TWFE as the headline. Use an estimator that respects who is a valid control.

Units all adopt at the same time → Day 1’s method is still correct, and you need none of this.

Problem Tool
already-treated units as controls csdid, did_imputation, did2s
contaminated event-study leads eventstudyinteract (Sun & Abraham)
where did the weights go? bacondecomp
pre-trend tests underpowered Roth (2022)
parallel trends only nearly true honestdid (Rambachan & Roth)
treatment turns on and off again did_multiplegt_dyn (de Chaisemartin & D’Haultfœuille)
treatment is a dose, not on/off Callaway, Goodman-Bacon & Sant’Anna

Where to read next

  • Roth (2022), AER: Insights — pre-trend testing. Read this one first.
  • Goodman-Bacon (2021), J. Econometrics — the decomposition you ran.
  • Callaway & Sant’Anna (2021), J. Econometrics — the estimator behind csdid.
  • Sun & Abraham (2021), J. Econometrics — contaminated leads.
  • Rambachan & Roth (2023), REStud — sensitivity analysis, not pre-testing.
  • de Chaisemartin & D’Haultfœuille, AER (2020) + REStat (2024) — treatments that switch on and off, or change in steps (not just 0/1); their command is did_multiplegt_dyn.
  • Callaway, Goodman-Bacon & Sant’Anna, AER (forthcoming) — DiD with a continuous treatment: a dose, not a switch.
  • Roth, Sant’Anna, Bilinski & Poe (2023) — the survey; use its flowchart.

You leave with the full project: data, do-files, handouts — a template to adapt to your own research. The assignment (next slides) uses it.

The assignment

The exercises

Work in groups: one do-file per group, top to bottom, written answers in comments; submit the .do and its .log before you leave.

  1. Confirm the diagnosis. Re-run the static TWFE using only the 2007 cohort and the never-treated districts. Compare it to Day 1’s 5.59 and to today’s 0.10. Which comparisons did dropping the other cohorts remove?
  2. Never-treated only. Re-run csdid without the notyet option. Compare the point estimate and the standard error. What did notyet buy, and what did it cost?
  3. Report it. Produce one table with all three of today’s estimates, plus the two-sentence caveat you would put under it in a policy brief for a ministry that has not read Goodman-Bacon.
  4. Break it, then fix it. Build the Day 2 table using estat simple followed by esttab ., and confirm the r(111) error. Then fix it with agg(simple). Better to meet this error today than at midnight.
  5. Run the whole thing (optional, for your own time). Delete everything in output/, run master.do, and confirm it all comes back identical. (Expected exception: .rtf files embed the time they were written.)
